sm: The host introduces Jeff Smith, director of the Heritage Foundation's Asian Studies Center, to discuss Nvidia, which controls nearly ninety percent of the data center GPU market. Smith describes a spy scandal in which CEO Jensen Huang was reportedly linked romantically to Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspede who US intelligence believes worked for China's MSS, possibly as a honey trap. Smith says the bigger scandal is how Nvidia chips flow to Chinese companies with almost no oversight. He argues frontier AI models, such as Anthropic's Mythos finding unknown cyber vulnerabilities, would give China major espionage advantages if it got there first.

Smith says there is also an economic angle, because compute is scarce and American companies, including Elon Musk, Dell and OpenAI, are begging for chips and memory. He argues the government should restrict dual-use technology to China just as it would missiles or fighter jets, and that doing so would not cost Nvidia profit since demand exceeds supply. He then rebuts the arguments made by Huang and Nvidia allies. First, he says Chinese military entities have been found seeking and using Nvidia chips. Second, he disputes the claim that China is only nanoseconds behind, and begins to define compute as how much processing power a chip delivers.

Smith says independent estimates put US compute production at about twenty times China's, with the gap possibly growing, so the claim that the two are neck and neck is false. On the argument that selling chips keeps China addicted and starves Huawei, he says Xi Jinping set a self-sufficiency goal for semiconductors back in 2015, and China will drop Nvidia once it no longer needs it. He calls such honeypot operations a common problem but unusual here because of Huang's prominence and his access to the president. He adds that Huang lobbied to ease export controls while chips went to Megaspede, which allegedly smuggled them to China. The government raised concerns in 2025, and Nvidia replied that it found nothing wrong.

Smith says a Bloomberg investigation found Megaspede was misreporting its inventory and could not account for fifty thousand Nvidia chips. He supports Heritage Action's backing of several bills, including the AI Overwatch Act, the Match Act and the Chip Security Act, covering global licensing with end-user checks, location verification built into chips, and limits on chipmaking equipment sales. He also describes smuggling cases, with the Justice Department revealing at least six in the past year. Sanctioned Chinese firms can also legally rent Nvidia chips through cloud providers in Southeast Asia. He says the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security has been asleep at the wheel and suspects unusual cooperation between parts of Commerce and Nvidia. He also says he would prioritize American customers first.
